(2024) explicitly say evasive bots could defeat their method if they learn to alter fingerprint attributes without introducing inconsistencies; they also note that stronger “unmodifiable” attributes would help detection but would raise privacy concerns. They further report that large-scale real-user evaluation was not feasible because reliable real-user ground truth is hard to obtain, and that temporal inconsistency checks can be bypassed by deleting cookies."},{"url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2606.14525v1","text":"Gundelach et al. (2026) say their scans came from one European datacenter at one point in time, covered only Tranco Top 10K homepages, and observed only explicit HTTP 403/429/503 blocks rather than degraded HTTP 200 responses. They also say they lacked a true human-browsing baseline, that their JavaScript proxies create detectable artifacts, and that observing an API probe does not prove the site blocked because of that probe."},{"url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2605.01247v1","text":"Wang et al. (2026) say their findings are limited by the coverage of browsing agents, tasks, and system configurations, and that future agents may adopt more human-like behaviors. They also warn that the lack of shared browser fingerprints between humans and agents in their dataset should not be read as proof that such overlap would not occur in practice."}],"weight":1}],"rejected_claims":[{"text":"All Chromium automation is trivially detectable in all settings.","reason":"The supplied evidence explicitly says the papers do not support that broad claim."},{"text":"Modern stealth Chromium is indistinguishable from humans.","reason":"The supplied evidence says it did not find recent primary evidence justifying that claim."},{"text":"Browser fingerprinting alone reliably catches all Chromium automation.","reason":"The supplied evidence says browser fingerprints alone can have limited power, especially for more human-like automation."}]}
